World Bank WDI panel prepared for LHWR examples

Source: R/data.R
wdi_lhwr.Rd

A country-year panel downloaded from the World Bank World Development Indicators API and included with the package as an illustrative real-data example for Lorentz Hyperbolic Weighted Regression. The data are real WDI observations for 2010–2024, but the Lorentz-hyperboloid representation is a documented demonstration of how raw economic variables can be converted into the Z matrix required by LHWR. It should therefore be treated as a package demo/template data set rather than as a definitive empirical application.

Format

A data frame with 2262 rows and 18 columns:

iso3

ISO 3-letter country code.

country

Country name.

region

World Bank region.

income_level

World Bank income group.

year

Calendar year, 2010–2024.

gdp_growth

Annual GDP growth, percent.

inflation

Annual inflation, percent.

fdi_gdp

Foreign direct investment net inflows, percent of GDP.

unemployment

Total unemployment, percent of labor force.

internet_users

Individuals using the Internet, percent of population.

school_secondary

Gross secondary-school enrollment, percent.

log_population

Natural logarithm of total population.

log_gdp_pc_const

Natural logarithm of constant-price GDP per capita.

trade_open

Trade openness, percent of GDP.

z0_lorentz

Positive time coordinate of the Lorentz representation.

z1_lorentz

First economic feature coordinate on the hyperboloid.

z2_lorentz

Second economic feature coordinate on the hyperboloid.

hyperboloid_error

Numerical check of the hyperboloid constraint plus one.

Source

World Bank World Development Indicators, downloaded through the API in July 2026 and distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license. Indicators include NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG, NY.GDP.PCAP.KD, NE.TRD.GNFS.ZS, BX.KLT.DINV.WD.GD.ZS, FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG, SP.POP.TOTL, SL.UEM.TOTL.ZS, IT.NET.USER.ZS, and SE.SEC.ENRR.

Details

The response and covariates are real-valued macroeconomic variables. The columns z0_lorentz, z1_lorentz, and z2_lorentz define a Lorentz-hyperboloid representation constructed from a two-component economic feature map. The frozen preprocessing constants are retained explicitly:

The index \(i\) identifies a country-year row. \(\mathrm{GDPpc}_i\) denotes positive constant-price GDP per capita and its natural logarithm is stored as log_gdp_pc_const. The first feature centers and scales that log:

$$ z_{i1} = \{\log(\mathrm{GDPpc}_i)-8.8071974413888245\}/1.4524958189486741, $$

The second feature centers and scales trade openness, measured as a percent of GDP in trade_open, using its separate frozen constants:

$$ z_{i2} = (\mathrm{trade\ openness}_i-91.8784599801564923)/58.6130974219034400, $$

Both spatial features are dimensionless. The positive time coordinate is then chosen to impose the unit-hyperboloid constraint:

$$ z_{i0} = \sqrt{1 + z_{i1}^2 + z_{i2}^2}. $$

Hence each row Z_i = (z0_lorentz, z1_lorentz, z2_lorentz) lies on the upper Lorentz hyperboloid. The coordinates satisfy -z0_lorentz^2 + z1_lorentz^2 + z2_lorentz^2 = -1 up to floating-point tolerance. The location and scale constants were calculated on the preprocessing reference sample before retaining this analysis panel. The coordinates are not longitude-latitude coordinates; they encode an economic neighborhood geometry based on GDP per capita and trade openness.

Examples

data(wdi_lhwr)
dat <- subset(wdi_lhwr, year == max(year))

# The package stores the constructed Lorentz coordinates directly.
Z <- as.matrix(dat[, c("z0_lorentz", "z1_lorentz", "z2_lorentz")])
check_hyperboloid(Z, stop_on_fail = TRUE)

# Reproduce the stored coordinates with the frozen preprocessing constants.
z1 <- (dat$log_gdp_pc_const - 8.8071974413888245) / 1.4524958189486741
z2 <- (dat$trade_open - 91.8784599801564923) / 58.6130974219034400
Z_rebuilt <- cbind(sqrt(1 + z1^2 + z2^2), z1, z2)
max(abs(Z - Z_rebuilt))

# Keep examples lightweight; use a modest grid.
fit_data <- data.frame(
  gdp_growth = dat$gdp_growth,
  unemployment = as.numeric(scale(dat$unemployment)),
  internet_users = as.numeric(scale(dat$internet_users))
)

bw <- bw.lhwr(
  gdp_growth ~ unemployment + internet_users,
  data = fit_data,
  Z = Z,
  approach = "AICc",
  bw_grid = c(40, 60),
  engine = "knn"
)
fit <- lhwr(
  gdp_growth ~ unemployment + internet_users,
  data = fit_data,
  Z = Z,
  bw = bw$bw,
  engine = "knn",
  diagnostics = "aicc"
)
fit
